tldr: By separating whole-body humanoid motor skills from environmental adaptation, and estimating physical dynamics from past interaction histories (context) to apply additional residual corrections, the authors propose a behavior foundation model capable of immediately adapting to heavy payloads and unseen environments without any test-time parameter updates.
hero_caption: Overall view of ECHO. A single pretrained behavior prior enables diverse teleoperated motions, ranging from acrobatic jumps to terrain adaptation. At the same time, even when loads are added to the limbs, it reads differences in the physical environment from interaction histories to achieve stable tracking and manipulation.
overview:
In recent years, behavior foundation models (BFMs) for humanoids combining large-scale motion imitation learning and reinforcement learning have attracted significant attention. However, when training a single model on diverse motions such as walking, fall recovery, and acrobatics, it cannot distinguish differences in friction or payload across environments. As a result, it settles on safe, conservative compromises that prevent collapse on average across all environments, fundamentally degrading precise motion tracking tailored to each specific environment.

To address this, the authors designed "ECHO", which separates general behavioral capability from adaptation to dynamics-specific execution. First, in the pretraining stage, they use a sampling method called "MIAS" that focuses practice on failure-prone, challenging motions while gradually shifting toward comprehensive coverage, allowing a single policy to acquire an extremely broad motion repertoire. Building on this, they trained an encoder to extract environment dynamics representations from the frozen prior's motion history (proprioception and past actions), along with a "residual policy" (a policy that learns corrections to the baseline behavior) that fine-tunes motor commands based on these representations.

Through experiments in simulation and on a real humanoid (Unitree G1), ECHO achieved motion tracking accuracy that outperformed even teacher models with privileged physical information, even under extreme dynamics changes such as heavy payloads. Furthermore, without any test-time weight updates, it successfully and robustly executed single-leg stands, squats, and real-time teleoperated motions while carrying a total of 10 kg of weights on its limbs.
contributions: Proposing "ECHO", an in-context behavior foundation model that separates broad motion tracking capability from dynamics-specific execution, enabling environmental adaptation without inference-time parameter updates.
Developing "MIAS", which balances targeted practice on difficult motions with comprehensive exploration to pretrain behaviors from acrobatics to ground contacts in a single stage.

Establishing "CRA", which learns motion-agnostic environment representations by combining multi-step lookahead prediction with neighborhood consistency in physical parameter space, correcting control via a residual policy.
Demonstrating adaptation to extreme heavy loads (a total of 10 kg across limbs), diverse terrains, and teleoperation of challenging acrobatics on a real Unitree G1 robot.

sections.heading: Why is it hard to balance humanoid dexterity with environmental adaptation?
sections.summary: Large-scale motion imitation has dramatically expanded humanoid behavioral repertoires, but covering diverse physical environments with a single policy sacrifices tracking accuracy. This paper introduces "ECHO", an in-context behavior foundation model that leverages interaction history as context to adapt to environment-specific control without test-time learning.
sections.details:
For humanoid robots to be useful in human society, they must execute diverse whole-body motions both agilely and robustly. Recently, behavior foundation models (BFMs) for whole-body control have advanced rapidly through reinforcement learning with large-scale motion capture data.

However, they hit a major roadblock. Even when attempting to imitate the same reference motion, the optimal joint torques or position commands to output differ completely if the robot carries weights on its limbs, encounters different floor friction, or faces changed actuator characteristics. If a single policy is trained without observing environmental physical parameters, the model learns a "safe compromise" to avoid falling in any environment, ultimately degrading motion sharpness and tracking fidelity.

To tackle this challenge, the authors focused on the robot's own "interaction history" (the history of past state transitions and actions). Looking at how the body responds to past commands inevitably reveals clues about the underlying physical environment (such as mass or friction). Therefore, while freezing the baseline whole-body policy (behavior prior), they proposed "ECHO", an in-context adaptation framework that estimates environmental dynamics from history and performs additional control corrections based on that information.

captions.F1: Real-robot demonstrations with ECHO. (a) Acrobatic jumps and backflips, (b) stair climbing and contact motions on slopes, and (c) manipulation and single-leg stands with weights attached to arms and legs. A single framework stably executes a wide variety of tasks.

sections.heading: Trends in behavior foundation models and in-context learning
sections.summary: This section surveys whole-body humanoid control models and dynamics adaptation techniques in robotics. ECHO is unique in combining broad skill pretraining with a residual adaptation approach driven by interaction histories.
sections.details:
Two major research streams form the foundation of this work.

### Behavior Foundation Models (BFMs)
Aiming for reusable foundations for whole-body motion, researchers are actively exploring diverse interfaces using generative models and improving tracking capabilities using large-scale data and parallel reinforcement learning (such as SONIC and HoloMotion-1). Additionally, models specialized for specific skills have emerged, such as HEFT for heavy payload transport and Extreme-RGMT for extreme agility. However, these remain focused on particular skills. ECHO unifies these diverse skills into a single policy using MIAS, described later.

### In-Context Learning and Dynamics Adaptation
Methods that adapt to tasks or environments from prompts or interaction histories without rewriting model weights at test time have progressed rapidly. For quadrupedal robots, approaches like RMA that distill privileged information or leverage proprioceptive histories are well known. However, in large-scale humanoid motion tracking, acquiring structured physical dynamics representations that do not depend on the motion type and pairing them with a residual policy had not been established. ECHO successfully captures pure physical representations uncorrupted by motion differences by combining world-model-style future prediction with neighborhood consistency learning.

sections.heading: The architecture of ECHO: Broad prior acquisition and history-based residual adaptation
sections.summary: ECHO consists of two components: acquiring a broad behavior prior "ECHO-PRE" via sampling that emphasizes challenging motions (MIAS), and introducing "CRA" to extract environmental dynamics from history and correct control.
sections.details:
Figure F2 shows the overall architecture. Let's walk through the formulation and training steps.

### 3.1 Problem Formulation
The task is formulated as reinforcement learning where environmental parameters $c$ (mass, friction, payload, etc.) cannot be directly observed. The robot acts based on its proprioception (joint angles, angular velocities, etc.) and target motion. In addition, past state and action histories $\mathcal{H}_t = (s_{t-H:t-1}^p, a_{t-H:t-1})$ are fed into an encoder $E_\varphi$ to generate an environmental latent variable $z_t = E_\varphi(\mathcal{H}_t)$, and the policy $\pi(a_t \mid s_t^p, m_t, z_t)$ outputs adaptive actions.

### 3.2 Pretraining a General Behavior Prior via MIAS
As the foundation for adapting to diverse environments, the robot first learns a behavior prior "ECHO-PRE ($\pi_\theta$)" that handles all motions without failing. Conventional uniform sampling often fails on difficult motions. To solve this, MIAS (Mixed and Annealed Sampling) is introduced.
- **Failure-Adaptive Sampling**: Reference motions are divided into time bins, and difficult segments are sampled preferentially using a weighted probability distribution $p^{\mathrm{A}}$ based on past failure rates $f_i$.
- **Mixed Sampling**: Three strategies are mixed depending on the situation: "rewind" (restarting from the beginning of the failed segment immediately after failure), "uniform exploration" across all motions, and "adaptive" based on failure rates (each with 1/3 probability upon failure).
- **Annealing**: As training progresses, the temperature parameter and probability bounds are gradually relaxed, removing bias toward specific motions and smoothly transitioning to uniform practice.

### 3.3 In-Context Adaptation via CRA
Next, the pretrained ECHO-PRE is frozen, and CRA (Context Representation and Residual Adaptation) is applied to infer the physical environment from history.
- **Short-term and Long-term Context**: It combines a short-term history $\mathcal{S}_t$ (50 steps / 1 second) capturing immediate responses with a long-term memory $\mathcal{M}_t$ accumulated from past motions within the same physical environment session.
- **Multi-step Prediction Loss**: To ensure the encoder $E_\varphi$ captures dynamics relevant to control, a predictor $D_\psi$ predicts privileged robot states and contact forces over the next $K_\mathrm{p}$ steps (loss $\mathcal{L}_\mathrm{pred}$).
- **Physical Neighborhood Soft Alignment**: To ensure latent representations are close for the same physical environment even across different motions, it minimizes the KL divergence between the Euclidean distance distribution in physical parameter space and the similarity distribution in latent space (loss $\mathcal{L}_\mathrm{soft}$).
- **Residual Adaptation**: With both the prior $\pi_\theta$ and encoder $E_\varphi$ completely frozen, only the residual policy $\pi_\Delta$, which takes latent variable $z_t$ as input, is trained via reinforcement learning. The final action is $a_t = a_t^\theta + a_t^\Delta$, fine-tuning environment-specific effort without compromising foundational motion capability.

captions.F2: Overview of ECHO's training architecture. (a) Pretraining with MIAS achieves balanced mastery across diverse motions, (b) context representations are learned from collected histories via future prediction and physical neighborhood alignment, and (c) both are frozen to train the residual policy in a clear three-stage pipeline.

sections.heading: Adaptation performance and representation quality validated in simulation and on hardware
sections.summary: Simulation verified tracking fidelity and environmental adaptation, confirming that learned representations linearly reflect physical parameters accurately. Furthermore, extreme heavy-load experiments on a real Unitree G1 robot validated the proposed method's effectiveness.
sections.details:
Experiments were conducted on the Unitree G1 using approximately 1,236 hours (over 220 million frames) of motion data.

### Motion Tracking Fidelity
Comparisons were made on unseen daily motions (AMASS-2000) and highly dynamic motions (BONES-SEED-100). Compared to ECHO-PRE w/o MIAS using uniform sampling, ECHO-PRE with MIAS outperformed existing HEFT and SONIC v1.1 in both success rate (SR) and mean per-joint position error (MPJPE). Furthermore, applying CRA in ECHO-N lowered tracking error even further under nominal conditions.

### Context Adaptation
Under a harsh domain randomization environment (HDR) where up to a total of 13 kg of load is applied to the limbs, ECHO was compared with a teacher model using privileged information (RMA-Teacher), its distilled student (RMA-Student), Any2Track using history latents, and Vanilla without residual representations. ECHO-H achieved a 98.1% success rate in HDR, surpassing even privileged RMA-Teacher (97.15%) to record top accuracy. While Any2Track showed no clear advantage over Vanilla, ECHO demonstrated marked tracking improvements.

### Representation Analysis and Context Length Scaling
When testing whether physical parameters could be read from learned latents using linear probes (Ridge regression), it achieved high coefficients of determination: $R^2 = 0.8357$ for payload mass and $R^2 = 0.9208$ for friction coefficient. Ablations revealed that physical neighborhood consistency ($\mathcal{L}_\mathrm{soft}$) contributes to cross-motion consistency, while future prediction loss ($\mathcal{L}_\mathrm{pred}$) directly enables linear decodability of physical quantities. Moreover, scaling context length from 1 second (50 steps) to 9 seconds (450 steps) monotonically improved environment identification accuracy and mass decoding accuracy.

### Real-Robot Experiments
In real-robot teleoperation on Unitree G1, challenging motions including crawling, stair climbing, and backflips succeeded. In motion tracking tests with 2 kg weights attached to each shin, ECHO-H achieved the lowest joint position error, demonstrating the adaptability to execute single-leg stands, forward bends, and squats without falling even under a total 10 kg load on its limbs.

captions.F4: Performance trends and t-SNE visualizations when scaling context length (interaction history duration) from 1 second to 9 seconds. Longer histories monotonically improve environment identification accuracy and payload estimation accuracy ($R^2$), and t-SNE shows samples from the same environment clustering far more distinctly than in Any2Track.

sections.heading: Deployment to a real robot: Can it move without falling even with attached weights?
sections.summary: Using a real Unitree G1, the authors evaluated teleoperation of broad pretrained whole-body skills and in-context adaptation behavior under added payloads. The robot confirmed proper posture correction against sudden load changes without any test-time updates.
sections.details:
Real-robot validation was conducted from two perspectives: skill breadth and environmental adaptation.

### Teleoperating Diverse Whole-Body Behaviors
Unitree G1 with ECHO-PRE successfully tracked behaviors involving severe dynamics—such as seamless transitions between standing and ground postures, climbing onto elevated platforms, and mid-air flips—using only a single trained model (Figure F6). This demonstrates that one foundation model can cover broad whole-body control without needing separate task-specific policies.

### Online Payload Adaptation
Various tasks were tested with weights attached to limbs, including manipulation (such as tabletop block arrangement), squats, single-leg stands, and standing up from seiza (kneeling). Particularly interesting was the moment weights like baskets were hung onto or removed from the robot's arms. Even without parameter updates, the robot instantly sensed the load from interaction history (context) after the arm sagged, autonomously pulling the arm back to the reference height (Figure F7). Quantitative evaluation also showed that ECHO-H achieved the lowest tracking error among baselines across all four motions with weights on both lower legs.

captions.F7: In-context adaptation on the real Unitree G1 robot. The top row shows precise object manipulation with wrist loads, the middle row shows single-leg stands and standing up with limb loads, and the bottom row illustrates the corrective process where the arm autonomously recovers its posture the instant a load is hung on it.

sections.heading: Future challenges and remaining limitations
sections.summary: Despite ECHO's strong adaptive capabilities, several realistic limitations and future directions are discussed, including reliance on simulation, handling abrupt intra-session environmental shifts, and generalizability to other robots.
sections.details:
The authors candidly note the following limitations:

- **Dependence on Simulation and Privileged Information**: Learning context representations requires rollouts in simulator environments and supervisory signals from privileged states (such as contact forces). Further verification is needed to determine how well it generalizes to unseen physical phenomena far outside the randomization range during training.
- **Handling Dynamic Intra-Session Changes**: The current memory mechanism assumes physical parameters remain constant within the same session and flushes history at episode boundaries. If friction or weight suddenly changes unannounced mid-session, accumulated past history could cause incorrect adaptation, pointing to a need for change-aware memory management.
- **Extending to Other Robots and Autonomous Tasks**: Experiments are limited to the Unitree G1, and the method focuses on tracking reference motions. Transferring to different robot morphologies and directly coupling with high-level task planning models (such as VLMs) remain future research directions.

takeaways: Explicitly separating a foundation model's motion repertoire (prior) from environment-specific control (residual adaptation) allows both broad behavioral coverage and high tracking fidelity.

Learning future state predictions and physical parameter neighborhood consistency from past motion histories (proprioception and actions) yields pure physical representations independent of motion types.
Scaling and accumulating context length (history duration) across several seconds monotonically improves physical parameter estimation accuracy, visibly stabilizing humanoid control.
Combining a residual policy with suitable context representations enables adaptation to harsh heavy loads on a real robot without test-time online fine-tuning or privileged information distillation.
limitations: Because training requires privileged simulation information (such as contact forces and exact mass parameters), limitations remain for phenomena with very large Sim-to-Real gaps.
If physical parameters change abruptly during a session, long-term past memory can become noise or bias, risking delayed adaptation or failure.
Validation is limited to the Unitree G1 and motion tracking tasks; zero-shot transfer to unseen robot morphologies and integration with high-level autonomous decision-making remain unverified.
